title: Modeling the Impact of Alternative Strategies for Rapid Molecular Diagnosis of Tuberculosis in Southeast Asia
abstract: Novel diagnostic tests hold promise for improving tuberculosis (TB) control, but their epidemiologic impact remains uncertain. Using data from the World Health Organization (2011-2012), we developed a transmission model to evaluate the deployment of 3 hypothetical TB diagnostic tests in Southeast Asia under idealized scenarios of implementation. We defined diagnostics by their sensitivity for smear-negative TB and proportion of patients testing positive who initiate therapy ("point-of-care amenability"), with tests of increasing point-of-care amenability having lower sensitivity. Implemented in the public sector (35% of care-seeking attempts), each novel test reduced TB incidence by 7%-9% (95% uncertainty range: 4%-13%) and mortality by 20%-22% (95% uncertainty range: 14%-27%) after 10 years. If also deployed in the private sector (65% of attempts), these tests reduced incidence by 13%-16%, whereas a perfect test (100% sensitivity and treatment initiation) reduced incidence by 20%. Annually detecting 20% of prevalent TB cases through targeted screening (70% smear-negative sensitivity, 85% treatment initiation) also reduced incidence by 19%. Sensitivity and point-of-care amenability are equally important considerations when developing novel diagnostic tests for TB. Novel diagnostics can substantially reduce TB incidence and mortality in Southeast Asia but are unlikely to transform TB control unless they are deployed actively and in the private sector.

summary.oneLiner: A transmission model suggests novel TB diagnostics could cut incidence and mortality in Southeast Asia, but only substantially with private-sector and active deployment.
summary.overview: Tuberculosis (TB) is an infectious disease, and better diagnostic tests could help control it if they find cases quickly and get patients onto treatment. The authors built a transmission model using World Health Organization data from 2011-2012 to simulate three hypothetical new TB tests in Southeast Asia under idealized rollout conditions. When deployed only in the public sector, which handles about 35% of care-seeking attempts, each test reduced TB incidence by 7%-9% and mortality by 20%-22% after 10 years. Deploying the tests in the private sector as well, which handles about 65% of attempts, increased the incidence reduction to 13%-16%. The authors conclude that such tests can substantially reduce TB but are unlikely to transform control unless they are deployed actively and in the private sector.
summary.question: How much could novel TB diagnostic tests, differing in sensitivity and point-of-care amenability, reduce TB incidence and mortality in Southeast Asia under different deployment strategies?
summary.method: A transmission model was developed to evaluate the deployment of 3 hypothetical TB diagnostic tests under idealized scenarios of implementation. Tests were defined by their sensitivity for smear-negative TB (a measure of how often the test catches cases that standard sputum smear microscopy misses) and by the proportion of positive patients who start therapy ("point-of-care amenability"). Tests with greater point-of-care amenability had lower sensitivity. Scenarios compared public-sector deployment, combined public and private deployment, a perfect test, and targeted screening that annually detects 20% of prevalent cases.
summary.data: Data from the World Health Organization for 2011-2012, applied to Southeast Asia. Public sector accounted for 35% of care-seeking attempts and private sector for 65%. Simulated outcomes were measured after 10 years. The abstract does not describe further sample details.
findings: Implemented in the public sector, each novel test reduced TB incidence by 7%-9% (95% uncertainty range: 4%-13%) and mortality by 20%-22% (95% uncertainty range: 14%-27%) after 10 years.
With private-sector deployment as well, the tests reduced incidence by 13%-16%.
A perfect test (100% sensitivity and treatment initiation) reduced incidence by 20%.
Annually detecting 20% of prevalent TB cases through targeted screening (70% smear-negative sensitivity, 85% treatment initiation) reduced incidence by 19%.
Sensitivity and point-of-care amenability are described by the authors as equally important considerations when developing novel TB diagnostics.
Novel diagnostics can substantially reduce TB incidence and mortality in Southeast Asia but are unlikely to transform TB control unless deployed actively and in the private sector.
summary.whyItMatters: The authors suggest that developers of TB diagnostics should weigh both sensitivity and point-of-care amenability, and that health programs should pursue active deployment and engage the private sector to achieve large gains. The findings are based on idealized implementation scenarios, so real-world impact may differ.
